name: Eleanor Roosevelt
role: American first lady (1933–1945), diplomat and human-rights activist
summary: Eleanor Roosevelt advocated democratic civil liberties, racial equality, labor protections and social provision. She worked for international human-rights institutions and peace, while taking specific positions on Israel, colonialism and refugees that were not reducible to a single universal rule.

notes: No inferred answers. Full Sorbonne speech, selected complete late My Day columns, correspondence and published question-and-answer text were downloaded or read and searched across themes. Sources cover her pre-White House activism, New Deal and wartime work, UN service and final years. The complete 490-statement list and remaining unknowns were checked; broad UDHR sponsorship is not assigned as automatic agreement with every article or every modern rights policy. Personal relationships do not establish positions on marriage or sexual law. Sanger advocacy does not establish abortion, eugenics or coercive population policy. Her later ERA position became less oppositional; it is not conflated with a view on every sex-specific law. She supported WWII and UN collective security, so late disarmament advocacy is not treated as categorical pacifism or unilateral nuclear disarmament. The Rosenberg record and use of both direct action and electoral action are retained as mixed evidence. Her claims about the causes of Palestinian displacement are her argument, not adopted historical findings. Some GWU headings and body publication dates differ by one day; URLs identify the precise text. No modern technology or climate-policy positions inferred from general concern for peace and conservation. Deepening pass (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-10-31) on line 14, from full My Day and If You Ask Me texts at the Eleanor Roosevelt Papers Project: rehabilitation, tariffs, the two-term limit, the Electoral College, possessions and population added. Searched without a usable answer: international criminal courts (her 1960 Eichmann column concerns a trial in Israel, not an international court; her Judgment at Nuremberg column reviews a film), deficits (1952 column only questions campaign promises of a balanced budget), nature for its own sake (1954 national-parks column defends beauty and undisturbed wildlife for visitors and resources), duty of the privileged (columns found concern the duty of the United States as a nation), gradual change (columns on desegregation timetables describe pace rather than a principle). Not in the local corpora (no UN general-debate speeches by her).
